references.topic: Impact of scope changes on fees, schedule, and financing.

questions.stem:
An architect has a $560,000 stipulated fee for a 40,000 sf medical office building. Halfway through design development, the owner adds 8,000 sf (a 20% increase in area). The architect calculates the additional fee from these assumptions:

- Remaining phases (half of DD, plus CD, procurement and CA) are 75% of the fee, and their effort scales with area
- Redesign of completed SD and DD work: 60 hours at $150

What additional fee should the architect propose?

options.explanation: This leaves out the redesign of completed work.
This scales the whole fee, including phases already complete.
This scales the whole fee and adds the redesign.

questions.stem:
During construction documents for a branch bank, the owner asks to add a second drive-through lane and a night-deposit vault. The architect estimates three weeks of added CD work on the critical path. The owner's construction loan commitment requires construction to start by a fixed date, now only four weeks after the current permit-submittal date.

What should the architect do? Check the three that apply.

options.text: Notify the owner in writing of the fee and schedule impacts
options.explanation: Correct. The owner needs the impacts in writing to decide.

options.text: Get the owner's written authorization before proceeding
options.explanation: Correct. This change in the owner's instructions is an additional service that needs authorization first.

options.text: Show how the change affects the loan's start deadline
options.explanation: Correct. The financing deadline makes the schedule impact critical to the owner's decision.

options.text: Absorb the redesign to protect the owner's schedule
options.explanation: Absorbing the fee doesn't remove the three weeks, and gives up compensation.

options.text: Proceed with the change and bill it at the end of CDs
options.explanation: Authorization must come before the work.

options.text: Ask the building department to shorten its review
options.explanation: The architect doesn't control agency review times.

questions.explanation: Scope changes: written impacts (fee, schedule, financing), then authorization before proceeding.

questions.stem:
A developer's lender will lend 70% of total project cost for a mixed-use building, up to a maximum loan of $12,000,000. The original total project cost was $16,000,000. During design development, the developer adds a rooftop amenity deck that increases the total project cost by $1,600,000. The developer asks how much more of its own equity it will need.

How much additional equity will the developer need?

options.explanation: This applies the 30% equity share to the increase and ignores the loan cap.
Correct. 70% of $17,600,000 is $12,320,000, but the loan is capped at $12,000,000. Equity rises from $4,800,000 to $5,600,000.
This is 70% of the increase, the amount the lender would fund without a cap.
This assumes the loan doesn't increase at all.

questions.stem:
The owner approved the construction documents for a university residence hall two weeks ago. The owner now wants to change the roofing from a single-ply membrane to a vegetated roof over half the building. The architect is preparing to advise the owner on the change before the documents go out for permit.

Which impacts should the architect evaluate? Check the four that apply.

options.text: Change in construction cost
options.explanation: Correct. The vegetated roof changes cost, including structure and drainage.

options.text: Architect and consultant fees for the revisions
options.explanation: Correct. Revising approved documents is an additional service.

options.text: Schedule effect, including permit timing
options.explanation: Correct. Redesign and structural changes may delay the permit submittal.

options.text: Effect on the owner's budget and funding
options.explanation: Correct. The owner needs to know whether funding covers the change.

options.text: Change in the architect's firm overhead rate
options.explanation: The firm's overhead isn't a project impact of the change.

options.text: The contractor's profit margin on the roof
options.explanation: No contractor is engaged yet, and its margin isn't the architect's to evaluate.

questions.explanation: Evaluate every scope change for cost, fee, schedule and financing.

questions.stem:
An owner's late program change will delay the start of construction of a $20,000,000 office building by six weeks. The owner's cost consultant uses 5% annual escalation. The owner also pays $25,000 per week to extend its lease in its current building until the new one is ready, and the completion date will slip by the same six weeks.

About what is the cost of the delay to the owner?

options.explanation: This counts escalation only and leaves out the lease extension.
This counts the lease extension only and leaves out escalation.
This applies a full year of escalation and adds the lease.

questions.stem:
An architect's stipulated fee for a corporate campus is $900,000. During construction documents, the owner deletes the fitness pavilion, about 10% of the construction cost. The architect had completed the pavilion's SD and DD and about a quarter of its CDs. The owner proposes cutting the fee by 10% ($90,000).

How should the architect respond?

options.text: Accept the 10% reduction to preserve the relationship
options.explanation: A straight cut ignores work already done on the pavilion.

options.text: Propose an equitable adjustment that credits work already done
options.explanation: Correct. The fee should reflect services already performed on the deleted portion and the reduced remaining effort.

options.text: Decline any reduction because the fee is a stipulated sum
options.explanation: A significant scope change justifies an adjustment, in either direction.

options.text: Bill the full pavilion fee as an additional service
options.explanation: The deletion reduces remaining work, so billing more isn't justified.

questions.explanation: Deletions on a stipulated sum: an equitable adjustment that credits completed work.

questions.stem:
The owner of a clinic authorized redesign of the waiting area as an hourly additional service with a not-to-exceed amount of $30,000. The architect's time records for the work are below, and no reimbursable expenses were incurred.

- Principal: 20 hours at $220
- Project architect: 80 hours at $150
- Designer: 120 hours at $110

What amount should the architect bill?

options.explanation: This leaves out the principal's hours.
The NTE is a ceiling, not the amount to bill.
This bills all 220 hours at the project architect's rate.

questions.explanation:
1. Principal = 20 × $220 = $4,400
2. Project architect = 80 × $150 = $12,000
3. Designer = 120 × $110 = $13,200
4. Total = $29,600 (under the $30,000 cap)

questions.stem:
Over three months of design development for a boutique hotel, the owner's team asked for about 25 small revisions: a moved wall, a changed finish, a second lobby option. Each took a few hours. The project manager just found that together they consumed 14% of the DD fee, and none was submitted as an additional service.

What should the project manager do going forward?

options.text: Keep absorbing small requests to maintain goodwill
options.explanation: Continuing to absorb the requests repeats the overrun.

options.text: Log requests and submit regular additional-service requests in advance
options.explanation: Correct. Tracking requests and getting authorization before the work protects the fee and keeps the owner informed.

options.text: Refuse all further owner revisions during DD
options.explanation: Some revisions are normal design iteration. The issue is tracking and authorization.

options.text: Bill all 25 past requests at the end of the project
options.explanation: Billing late, without prior notice or authorization, invites disputes.

questions.explanation: Track small changes and get authorization before doing them.

questions.stem:
During construction of a library, the owner has requested 12 changes. For each one, the architect must evaluate the contractor's pricing and supporting data and revise drawings, which has taken about 40 hours so far. The contractor needs answers quickly to avoid delaying the work.

How should the architect handle this work?

options.text: Stop evaluating the changes until the owner authorizes a fee
options.explanation: Stopping during construction risks delay. The agreement has the architect proceed and notify.

options.text: Proceed to avoid delay and promptly notify the owner
options.explanation: Correct. Evaluating change proposals and revising documents are services provided to avoid delay, with prompt notice (§4.2.3).

options.text: Absorb the work within basic CA services
options.explanation: Evaluating proposals and revising documents is an additional service.

options.text: Have the contractor prepare the revised drawings
options.explanation: The architect is responsible for revising its own instruments of service.

questions.explanation: §4.2.3: provide the service to avoid delay, and notify promptly.

flashcards.back: Bill the actual hours × rates, up to the cap. The cap isn't the bill.

Escalation over the delay + carrying costs (rent, interest, lost revenue).
Cost added above the cap is all owner equity.
